en: Majjhima Nikāya 87,
Piyajātika Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain householder had lost his only son, who was dear and beloved.
Because of his death, neither his business affairs nor his food appealed to him.
So he went to the cremation ground and wailed:
“Where are you, my only son? Where are you, my only son?
Then that householder approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, your faculties are not established in your own mind; there is a transformation in your faculties.
“But how could my faculties not be transformed, venerable sir?
For my only son, dear and beloved, has passed away.”
“With his passing away, neither my work nor my food seems possible to me.
Having gone to the cremation ground, I weep:
‘Where are you, my only son? Where are you, my only son?’”
“Just so, householder, just so, householder.
For sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from those who are dear, arise from those who are dear.
“But who, Bhante, would think such a thing?”
“Are sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair born of what is dear, produced by what is dear?
“Venerable sir, joy and happiness are indeed born of what is dear, produced by what is dear.
Then that householder, not rejoicing in the Blessed One’s words and criticizing them, rose from his seat and departed.
Now at that time, a number of dice-players were playing with dice not far from the Blessed One.
Then that householder approached those dice-players; having approached, he said this to the dice-players:

"Just now, sirs, I went to where the ascetic Gotama was; having approached and paid homage to the ascetic Gotama, I sat down to one side. As I was sitting there to one side, sirs, the ascetic Gotama said this to me:"
‘Householder, your faculties are not established in your own mind; there is a change in your faculties.
When this was said, sirs, I said this to the ascetic Gotama:
‘Venerable sir, how could there be no change in my faculties?’”
"Venerable sir, my only son, who was dear and beloved to me, has passed away.
Because of his death, neither work nor food appeals to me.
Having gone to the cremation ground, I weep:”
“Where are you, my only son? Where are you, my only son?
“It is even so, householder; it is even so, householder.
For sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of those who are dear, arise from those who are dear.”
“Venerable sir, who would think that sorrow,
lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of those who are dear,
produced by those who are dear? For, venerable sir, it is joy and happiness that are born of those who are dear, produced by those who are dear.”
"Then, sirs, not approving of the ascetic Gotama’s speech and criticizing it, I rose from my seat and departed.
"It is so, householder, it is so, householder.
For joy and gladness, householder, are born of what is dear and originate from what is dear."
Then that householder, thinking, "I am on equal terms with the gamblers," departed.
Subsequently, this subject of conversation gradually reached the royal palace.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed Queen Mallikā:
“Mallikā, this was said by the ascetic Gotama:
‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of those who are dear; they arise from those who are dear.
“If this was spoken by the Blessed One, O Great King, it is so.”
“In the same way, whatever the ascetic Gotama says, Mallikā approves of it all, saying:
‘If this was spoken by the Blessed One, Great King, it is indeed so.
It is just as when a teacher says something to his pupil, and the pupil approves of it all.”
‘So it is, teacher; so it is, teacher.
In the same way, Mallikā, whatever the ascetic Gotama says, you applaud it all, saying:
‘If this was spoken by the Blessed One, Great King, then it is so.’”
“Worse than that, Mallikā! You shall perish!
Then Queen Mallikā addressed the brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha:

“Come, brahmin, go to where the Blessed One is; having approached him, pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, and inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, strength, and well-being.”
‘Venerable sir, Queen Mallikā pays homage with her head at the Blessed One’s feet; she inquires after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, strength, and well-being.
And say this as well:
‘Venerable sir, has this word been spoken by the Blessed One:’”
“Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of those who are dear, arise from those who are dear.
Having thoroughly grasped whatever the Blessed One explains to you, report it to me;
for Tathāgatas do not speak untruthfully.
“Yes, lady,” Nāḷijaṅgha the brahmin replied to Queen Mallikā. He then approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, Nāḷijaṅgha the brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

“Lady Mallikā, Master Gotama, pays homage with her head at the feet of Master Gotama. She inquires after your health, your freedom from affliction, your lightness of being, your strength, and your well-being.”
And he says this:
“Venerable sir, has this word been spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from those who are dear, arise from those who are dear’?”
“So it is, brahmin; so it is, brahmin.
For grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair are born of those who are dear, arise from those who are dear.
This can be understood, brahmin, by this method as well: how grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair are born of those who are dear, arise from those who are dear.”
Once upon a time, brahmin, in this very Sāvatthī, the mother of a certain woman passed away.
Because of her death, she became insane and deranged; wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, she would say:
“Have you seen my mother? Have you seen my mother?”
"By this method also, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear and originate from what is dear.
Once in the past, brahmin, the father of a certain woman here in Sāvatthī died...
her brother died..."
A sister died...
a son died...
a daughter died...
Her husband passed away.
Because of his death, she became insane and deranged; wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, she said this:
"Have you seen my husband? Have you seen my husband?"
"By this method, too, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, originate from what is dear.
Once upon a time, brahmin, in this very Sāvatthī, a certain man’s mother died.
Because of her death, he became mad and deranged; wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, he would say: [text continues]"
‘Did you see my mother? Did you see my mother?
By this method also, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of those who are dear, arise from those who are dear.
Once in the past, brahmin, the father of a certain man in this very Sāvatthī passed away…
A brother has passed away… a sister has passed away… a son has passed away…
His daughter died...
his wife died.
Because of her death, he became insane and deranged; wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, he spoke thus:
‘Did you see my wife? Did you see my wife?
By this method, too, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, arise from what is dear.
Once in the past, brahmin, a certain woman from this very Sāvatthī went to her relatives’ home.
Her relatives, having deprived her husband of her, wished to give her to another;
but she did not desire him.
Then that woman said this to her husband:
“Noble son, these relatives of mine wish to take you away from me and give you to another,
yet I do not desire that for you. Then that man cut the woman in two and tore himself apart.
‘Both of us shall exist after death.
It is by this method, brahmin, that it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear and originate from what is dear.
Then the brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat.

He approached Queen Mallikā; having approached her, he reported to Queen Mallikā in its entirety the entire conversation that had taken place with the Blessed One. Then Queen Mallikā approached King Pasenadi of Kosala;
having approached him, she said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“What do you think, Great King,
is Princess Vajirī dear to you?
“Yes, Mallikā, Princess Vajirī is dear to me.”
“What do you think, Great King?
Would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you from the change and alteration of the princess Vajirī?
“Mallikā, from the change and alteration of the princess Vajirī, even my life itself would be altered; how then could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?”
“This, great king, is what was said by that Blessed One—knowing and seeing, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One—with reference to this:
‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of the beloved; they arise from the beloved.
What do you think, great king?”
“Are the Vāsabha Khattiyas dear to you?
“Yes, Mallikā, the Vāsabha Khattiyas are dear to me.
“What do you think, Great King? Would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you from the change and alteration of the Vāsabha Khattiyā?”

“Mallikā, if only through the change and alteration of my noble wife Vāsabhā, there might be a change even in my life itself; how then could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?
“It was with reference to this, Great King, that the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One—said:
‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of the beloved, produced by the beloved.’”
“What do you think, Great King, is the general Viṭaṭūbha dear to you?
“Yes, Mallikā, the general Viṭaṭūbha is dear to me.
“What do you think, Great King, would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you through the change and alteration of the general Viṭaṭūbha?”
“Mallikā, if there were a change and alteration in my general Viṭaṭūbha, there might even be a change in my life; how then could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?
“It was with reference to this, Great King, that the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—spoke thus:
‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of those things that are dear; they originate from those things that are dear.’”
“What do you think, Great King, am I dear to you?
“Yes, Mallikā, you are dear to me.
“What do you think, Great King?”
“Would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in me because of change and alteration?
“Indeed, Mallikā, because of change and alteration in you, there would even be a change in my life itself; how then could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?
“It was with reference to this, Great King, that the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—spoke thus.”
“Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of those who are dear, arise from those who are dear.
What do you think, Great King:
are Kāsī and Kosala dear to you?”
“In this way, Mallikā, Kāsī-Kosala is dear to me.
It is through the power of Kāsī-Kosala, Mallikā, that we enjoy Kāsī sandalwood and wear garlands, perfumes, and ointments.
“What do you think, Great King?”
“Would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you because of the change and alteration of Kāsī and Kosala?
“Mallikā, if there were change and alteration of Kāsī and Kosala, even my life itself would be subject to change; how then could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?
“It was with reference to this, Great King, that the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—spoke thus:”
“Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of those who are dear, arise from those who are dear.
“It is wonderful, Mallikā! It is marvelous, Mallikā!
To what an extent that Blessed One truly sees, having penetrated with wisdom!”
"Come, Mallikā, rinse your mouth.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
"Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!"
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The seventh discourse, “Born of Love,” is finished.
